title: The giant who was a musician
hook: the forest giant falls, remembers who he was, and shows a pattern Hindus see all through the Ramayana: the curse and its release
carry: the atman is never the curse it wears

segments.voice: Yesterday: tapas wins boons, but no boon beats dharma. Viradha, the giant no weapon can kill, seized Sita, until the brothers broke his arms.

Here's the problem. Viradha is down, arms broken, but no weapon can kill him. Brahma's boon still holds. So what do you do with an enemy who can't die the ordinary way? Rama tells Lakshmana to dig a pit, a deep one, big enough for a body that size. While Lakshmana digs, Rama puts his foot on Viradha's throat to hold him down. That's when the giant's face changes.
screen: `AN ENEMY WHO CAN'T DIE.` → `DIG A PIT.` → `THE GIANT'S FACE CHANGES.`

segments.voice: Viradha looks up and recognizes him. You're Rama, Kausalya's son. Then he tells his story. He wasn't always a forest giant. He was a gandharva, one of the celestial musicians, named Tumburu. He fell in love with the apsara Rambha, and in his longing he didn't come when Kubera, the lord of wealth, called for him. Kubera cursed him: become a rakshasa, a terror of the forest. Tumburu begged, and the curse was given a limit. When Rama, son of Dasharatha, kills you in battle, you'll return to heaven. So Viradha tells the brothers how to finish it. Bury me in a pit; that's the old way for one like me. And go to the sage Sharabhanga; he'll help you. As the earth covers him, he rises, released. Hindus know this shape well. A curse, a shapa, nearly always comes with its release, and the release is often meeting God. Ahalya, back in the first book, was freed when Rama came to her husband's hermitage. Viradha is freed today. Devotees read it as Rama's grace. And under it sits one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: the atman, the true self, isn't the body it's born into. A curse can give you a monster's form. It can't make the self a monster. That's why a Hindu grandmother, hearing about someone at their worst, might say: that's not who they are. The enemy was a soul waiting to be freed, and then he became the guide.
screen: `YOU'RE RAMA.` · `TUMBURU, A CURSED MUSICIAN.` · `BURY ME. GO TO SHARABHANGA.` · `A CURSE AND ITS RELEASE.` · then, large: `THE SELF WAS NEVER THE MONSTER.`

segments.voice: Many Hindu families know an old prayer: sarve bhavantu sukhinah, may all beings be happy, may all be well. Bring to mind someone who frightened or frustrated you this year, at a safe distance, without excusing anything. If you pray, say the prayer for them, slowly, a few times. If you don't, wish it quietly, and breathe until the picture softens a little.
Viradha. A gandharva named Tumburu, cursed to be a giant until Rama came. Buried, he rises free, and sends Rama to Sharabhanga.
Your line: the atman is never the curse it wears. Under the monster was a musician. Day five hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Hindu storytellers often point to Viradha as the first of several beings in the Ramayana released from a curse by meeting Rama, a pattern many devotees read as a sign of his grace.

Tumburu.meaning: the gandharva Viradha had been before the curse

Kubera.meaning: the lord of wealth, who cursed Tumburu

Rambha.meaning: an apsara, one of heaven's dancers

rakshasa.meaning: a demon of the epics, a terror of the forest

atman.meaning: the true self, which no curse or body can change

shapa.meaning: a curse, which in the stories comes with its release
